question.text: Mr. Ramesh Iyer, a product-strategy manager at Nilgiri Multi-Strategy Fund, wants to take an exposure to rent-yielding commercial real estate cash flows WITHOUT holding physical property. Chapter 2 classifies the instrument he will use as a 'DUAL' category (neither purely traditional nor purely alternative). Which instrument fits this description?

answer.text: A direct purchase of a 50,000 sq-ft office building on its own books
A limited-partnership stake in an unlisted real-estate private-equity fund
Units of a listed Real Estate Investment Trust (REIT) that are exchange-traded but underlying is real estate
A forward contract on a residential property index executed OTC with a single dealer

explanation.text: The Logic: Per Section 2.3.4 and Table 2.1, REITs (and InvITs) are classified in the DUAL category: the underlying assets are illiquid real-estate or infrastructure projects (alternative in nature), but the instrument itself is listed and liquid on the stock exchange (traditional feature). The chapter explicitly says REITs 'are sometimes considered either traditional assets or in the dual category.' The Trap: Option A is a direct real-estate holding — pure alternative/illiquid. Option B is a PE fund — pure alternative. Option D is a bilateral OTC derivative — an alternative/complex structure, not dual. The listed-status of REITs is what gives them the dual identity. Cross-Exam Context: XIX-A (Cat I/II Distributor) covers infra/real-estate AIFs as Cat I AIFs. XIX-E (here) reframes the same instruments from the Cat III manager's asset-allocation desk. Manager's Pro-Tip: Cat III funds routinely use REIT/InvIT units as liquid proxies for real-asset beta when the fund mandate permits listed instruments. Because the units are exchange-traded you can hedge them with single-stock futures where available, preserving daily NAV tractability — something you cannot do with a direct PE-stake in a real-estate SPV.
